A customer of ours asked us to fabricate a transition like this one 1, 2. 8" round to 7 1/2" × 9" rectangle, 22" long. They needed it rush, it failed and they were using an old one as a backup.

The original is cast iron with a wear resistant coating poured over it, it's part of a wood chip conveyor system. There's a blower behind the rectangular part and the wood chips get fed through the top by a belt conveyor, then it gets shot up about 4 stories high to get boiled.

We had to make 2 and the customer would then fit the flanges in place and do 1/8" of hard facing inside of it. The cost of the original was over 6k$ with a 4 month waiting period.

So after doing some quick math I traced out the rough pattern on 1/4" hot rolled steel, not ideal but it's what we had in stock for a rush, notice the color variation which I'll get back to later. I cut it on the shear so I could have a blank to trace the other 3.

Once that was done I clamped them all together and marked the bend lines and then traced them onto the blanks.

Then I turned on the press brake and punched in a few values, measured the steel thickness and ran a few tests on scraps to get the 157° I wanted.

So with 1/4" thick steel and a 35mm die, 1° of bending equals roughly 0.0056" of downwards movement, I had to make it go down roughly 0.014" more. The controller does most of the work but you still have to fiddle with it until you get it spot on.

Then I started bending the blanks and checking my progress along the way with a high quality gauge. That discoloration I mentioned earlier is the shitty part if hot rolled steel, it doesn't have the same hardness throughout the plate. So it doesn't bend equally, some areas have more resistance and spring back.

It was also impossible to get a 90° bend at the rectangular end following that pattern on a 35mm die.. So I put on a 3" V die with a bigger punch and gave it a proper 90° bend over a few inches.. Slight pressing was required afterwards to fine tune its shape.

Then I put 2 halves together and traced out the final shape so I could trim off the excess material..

Now it was down to welding so I tacked the ends together and did a quick edge prep 3/16th deep with a pipefitters blade. That way I only had to do a single pass on the outside & get complete joint penetration. Then I grinded down the ends and got those properly welded as well. Afterwards I let it cool down with the help of the ventilation and grinded it down to a smooth finish for the customer's own welders to finish off.

It took me a full day and half a sheet of steel to get it done, charged them around 1500$ iirc. With their own guys fitting the flanges and doing the hard facing the customer's final cost was still well below the 6000$ manufacturer's price tag.
